sentences.text: The name Dicraeosaurus refers to the distinctive neural spines located on the back of the animal's neck, a feature that set it apart from most other diplodocoids which typically possessed longer necks and smaller heads.

Unlike its relatives, this dinosaur had a relatively short, wide neck containing 12 unusually short vertebrae, measuring about 2.4 meters in length out of a total body length that could reach up to 20 meters.
The first fossils of Dicraeosaurus were described by paleontologist Werner Janensch in 1914.
Researchers suggest the tall neural spines likely provided attachment points for muscles, serving as insertion points for powerful neck muscles.

In 2008, Lehman and Woodward estimated that a mature adult Dicraeosaurus lived for 11 to 22 years and grew at an average rate of 227 to 455 kg per year, growing rapidly and without interruption to its maximum size, reaching sexual maturity at 80% of that maximum size.

Dicraeosaurus hansemanni lived between the Oxfordian and Kimeridgian stages, while D. sattleri lived during the Tithonian stage, with the genus living from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, approximately 161.5 to 143.1 million years ago.
A 2026 study by Beeston et al. included Dicraeosaurus sattleri in an analysis of caudal vertebrae that found at least five independent origins or reversals of pneumaticity in Neosauropoda.
